entries.root_cause: The initial G2 implementation policy treated repository location as sufficient capability authority. Broad sql/g2 and src/jlmirror_g2 prefixes allowed a candidate to place G3 inventory, parallel Monitoring persistence/domain truth, or replacement behavior inside an otherwise allowlisted path while the scope gate still reported success.
horizontal_audit: G2 path allowlist versus capability authority

entries.root_cause: The G2 authorization validator originally authenticated the privileged issue_comment workflow mostly through raw marker presence. Required validator invocations or fail-closed publication semantics could therefore be moved into comments or bypassed while the same strings remained in the file and authorization validation still passed.

Trusted G2 status evidence selected the latest row using created_at alone even though GitHub status timestamps have only second-level resolution. Two trusted statuses created in the same second could therefore be returned in an arbitrary order and allow an older success to be selected ahead of a newer pending or failure result.

The first semantic hardening still omitted the allowlisted implementation/g2-monitoring-source-onboarding namespace from semantic scanning. Executable Python or other code placed beside the implementation claim could therefore carry G3 inventory or parallel Monitoring persistence semantics while remaining inside a path accepted by the trusted scope evaluator.

The structural workflow validator proved that the trusted evaluator command existed as an active parsed shell command but did not prove unconditional reachability. An enclosing dead branch could preserve the expected command text while causing Bash to skip candidate evaluation and still let the analyze job complete successfully.

The semantic scan set still omitted the authorized tests/g2 prefix even though those Python or script artifacts can be imported or executed by G2 runtime code. A candidate could therefore hide parallel Monitoring persistence or G3 behavior in a test-named module while path admission and semantic validation both passed.

Semantic artifact inspection was gated by a finite filename-suffix allowlist. SQL, shell and extensionless executable text could remain inside an authorized prefix but skip forbidden-marker inspection entirely, allowing parallel Monitoring persistence or out-of-scope behavior to bypass the capability fence.

Forbidden capability markers were compared only in literal lowercase spellings. Equivalent camelCase, PascalCase or punctuation-free identifiers such as ResourceInventory and metricCurrentState therefore did not match snake-case markers and could encode excluded G3 behavior while passing semantic validation.

The trusted evaluator command check accepted any logical command beginning with the expected Python invocation. Appended shell status suppression preserved the prefix while converting an evaluator failure into a successful step, allowing final trusted publication to proceed despite rejected candidate scope.

The final publisher validator proved fail-closed state assignment and success-branch ordering but did not constrain later assignments to the worker result variable. A candidate workflow could overwrite result with success after state initialization and cause a failed analyze or readiness job to publish trusted success when live coordinates still matched.

The normalized semantic guard still relied on a partial denylist and therefore did not mechanically mirror every capability explicitly excluded by the G2 task packet. Alternate direct names could encode forbidden later-gate behavior under an authorized path while attestation passed.

Rejecting ordinary shell control-flow syntax was insufficient because shell name shadowing could preserve a canonical-looking evaluator invocation while preventing execution of the trusted interpreter.
Direct result assignment checks did not cover indirect shell mutation primitives, allowing result or state to be changed after fail-closed initialization and before trusted status publication.

Semantic normalization discarded non-ASCII code points instead of applying Unicode compatibility normalization first. Executable compatibility identifiers could therefore normalize at language runtime to a forbidden capability while the G2 semantic gate passed the candidate.

The semantic denylist still encoded some excluded capabilities only as compound spellings. Bare or alternate direct names could therefore implement explicitly excluded authority while passing attestation.

The workflow validator authenticated the trusted evaluator invocation exactly but only required the materialization command to appear somewhere in the worker job. Extra commands or steps could replace the base-owned evaluator between materialization and invocation.

Publisher assignment validation covered literal and indirect mutation primitives but not every shell assignment form. Alternate writes could change scalar expansion and forge trusted success after a failed worker.

Unicode compatibility normalization did not close cross-script confusable identifiers. Executable G2 artifacts could encode forbidden capability names with visually similar non-ASCII characters and evade ASCII marker extraction.

Resolve-job authority checks were authenticated by command presence rather than the complete canonical workflow object, leaving reachability dependent on shell structure not represented by the marker checks.

Worker validation constrained run scripts but did not authenticate the complete ordered YAML step set, so an additional non-run step could interpose between base-owned evaluator materialization and invocation.
The canonical final publisher path was validated but the workflow surface did not mechanically prohibit an additional status-publishing step after it.

Normalized substring matching made broad denylist words reject unrelated or authorized identifiers containing the same character sequence. The semantic fence therefore lacked an identifier boundary model and could block legitimate G2 implementation.

The semantic extractor evaluated ASCII source spelling literally and did not decode language-level Unicode identifier escapes. JavaScript and TypeScript could therefore encode a forbidden identifier entirely as ASCII escape syntax while the runtime resolved it to excluded G3 or credential authority.
horizontal_audit: invalid and surrogate escape fail-closed behavior

entries.root_cause: The confusable defense classified executable artifacts through a finite suffix allowlist. Executable or compilable governed formats outside that list, including component and future language files, could carry cross-script forbidden identifiers without triggering the non-ASCII fail-closed fence.

Token-boundary matching required exact normalized identifier equality and therefore missed ordinary morphological variants of explicitly excluded capabilities. Plural names such as Metrics, Problems and ResourceInventories could directly encode forbidden later-gate surfaces while still receiving trusted scope PASS.
horizontal_audit: false-positive regression for browser_automation and geometric_layout
